Stated Claim / Post Context:
My quest for peace and quiet

How sound subjectivity can make urban life challenging

Actual Article Body:
I hate noise. I leave my flat and I’m made to suffer the siren of e-bikes, the compensatory boom of souped-up cars, the midlife-crisis roar of a motorbike. I’m forced to overhear FaceTime on the train: digital chinwags to the detriment of everyone in the carriage and maybe the world. I have to attend meetings in open-plan offices, heightening visibility at the expense of my sanity. Even once-quiet sanctuaries are in freefall. Public libraries close early or have closed entirely. Coffee shops have developed a penchant for techno. Parks blast music all summer, our few remaining green spaces sold to the richest noisemaker.

Our homes are not much better. According to the most recent English Housing Survey (EHS)﻿, 46 per cent of households report noise problems, with 42 per cent of those households claiming noise affects their sleep. Traffic was the issue most commonly referenced in the survey, followed closely by street noise, caused by many of my nemeses: speakerphone-shouters, vlogging influencers, the bloke outside my flat the other day who hoisted a boombox like he was John bloody Cusack.

Excess noise is largely consigned to cities. But more people than ever live in cities—most of us, in fact—and they are loud. Decibel Shield, an app that measures sound in cities across the world, found four of the noisiest 10 are in India, many with average daytime noise above 80 decibels, akin to a hairdryer, and nighttime noise above 70, like a 24/7 hoover. London sits comfortably at number 40—a bit quieter than Chicago and Paris—but it is hardly quiet, with average daytime noise akin to a loud washing machine. I grew up in London and I still live there. I love my city, even with its excesses. But I wish I could turn it down.

Illustration by Mike Turner

I am not alone. Four-fifths of Brits value quiet time, according to a 2023 national noise repor﻿t by Quiet Mark, a noise certification company. Nearly two-thirds crave a quieter home. But it seems to be getting harder to live in one. The Chartered Institute of Environmental Health (CIEH) recently foun﻿d that nearly a third of Brits believe their area has grown louder in the past two years alone. And noise is not simply a matter of annoyance. According to the magazine Harvard Medicine, excessive noise exposure may cause memory impairment, learning delays, mental health problems and cardiovascular disease.
